excerpt: When a sprained ankle at work qualifies for workers' compensation, how to document it, who chooses your doctor, and the Georgia and South Carolina deadlines to report the injury and file a claim.
keyTakeaways: Report a work injury to a supervisor or manager right away: in Georgia no compensation is payable unless your employer gets notice within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80), and in South Carolina the limit is 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20). File your claim within one year of the injury in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82) and within two years of the accident in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). In both states a sprained ankle is covered only if it is an injury by accident arising out of and in the course of your employment. In Georgia you choose a doctor from your employer's posted panel of physicians; in South Carolina your employer chooses the treating doctor, and care you arrange on your own may not be paid. Medical records documenting when, where and how the injury happened are vital evidence in your claim.

faqs.question: When does a sprained ankle count as a work injury?
faqs.answer: When it is an injury by accident arising out of and in the course of your employment (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1(4); S.C. Code § 42-1-160(A)): the work has to be what caused it and it has to happen while you are doing your job. Twisting your ankle on a walk at home is not covered; spraining it on an uneven factory floor at work generally is.

faqs.question: What is the threshold requirement for a workers' compensation claim?
faqs.answer: Work-relatedness, which both Georgia and South Carolina define as an injury by accident 'arising out of and in the course of' employment (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1(4); S.C. Code § 42-1-160(A)). Both parts have to be true, and it is the question that has to be answered before the rest of the claim matters.

faqs.question: Why should I get medical treatment for a minor work injury?
faqs.answer: Because medical records are vital evidence, and because the bill is only covered if the right doctor treats you. In Georgia you choose from the employer's posted panel of at least six physicians and may switch once within it without Board approval (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201); in South Carolina the employer chooses the treating doctor and treatment you arrange on your own may not be paid (S.C. Code § 42-15-60(A)). Emergencies are the exception in both states. Treatment protects your recovery and documents when, where and how the injury happened.

faqs.question: Should I report a minor injury to my employer?
faqs.answer: Yes, and there is a deadline: in Georgia no compensation is payable unless the employer gets notice within 30 days of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80); in South Carolina the limit is 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20). Both statutes excuse a late report only in limited situations, such as the employer already knowing about the accident or not being prejudiced by the delay. Tell a supervisor or manager, not just a co-worker. Minor injuries sometimes turn out to be more serious, and a late report gives the insurer room to dispute the connection to work.

faqs.question: Does workers' compensation cover occupational illnesses too?
faqs.answer: Yes, but under a separate, stricter test. Both states exclude disease from the definition of 'injury' except where it results naturally and unavoidably from the accident, and compensate occupational disease under their own rules. Georgia requires proof of all five elements in O.C.G.A. § 34-9-280(2), including a direct causal connection between the work conditions and the disease and that it is not an ordinary disease of life to which the general public is exposed. South Carolina requires a disease 'due to hazards in excess of those ordinarily incident to employment' and peculiar to the occupation, and excludes ordinary diseases of life and chronic skeletal joint diseases (S.C. Code § 42-11-10). Those claims turn on connecting the condition to the hazards of the particular job rather than to one event.
